paragraphs: This paper addresses a practical tension: a model can make accurate predictions while remaining difficult to understand. Existing explanation methods offer different ways to assign importance to input features, but their relationships and relative advantages are often unclear. SHAP provides a shared framework for understanding these methods and explaining individual predictions.

The framework assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction. Its central theoretical contribution is to identify a class of additive feature importance measures and show that exactly one solution within that class satisfies a specified set of desirable properties. The uniqueness result is therefore tied to that class and those properties.

This perspective brings six existing methods into one framework and reveals that several lack the proposed properties. The authors also develop explanation methods informed by this analysis. These show improved computational performance, better agreement with human intuition, or both. The contribution combines a clearer basis for comparing explanations with practical methods for computing them.
neurips-2017-a-unified-approach-to-inter.tldr: SHAP unifies feature-attribution methods and identifies a unique additive explanation satisfying a specified set of desirable properties.

paragraphs: The paper studies greedy coordinate descent for optimization problems with l1 regularization, a setting associated with sparse solutions. Greedy coordinate descent selects coordinates to update according to their apparent usefulness. The authors seek to improve this approach by combining it with Nesterov acceleration and stochastic optimization.

The key step is a new greedy selection rule based on an approximation involving the squared l1 norm. Solving the resulting regularized approximation is nontrivial, although the problem is convex. The authors introduce SOTOPO, an efficient soft-thresholding projection algorithm that solves this subproblem exactly. That solver makes the new selection rule usable within an accelerated stochastic method.

The resulting algorithm, ASGCD, achieves the stated optimal convergence rate of O(sqrt(1/epsilon)). It also reduces the iteration complexity of greedy selection by up to a factor equal to the sample size. Theoretical analysis and experiments indicate better performance for high-dimensional, dense problems whose solutions are sparse. This identifies the particular combination of problem structure and solution structure where the approach is especially useful.
neurips-2017-accelerated-stochastic-gree.tldr: ASGCD combines a new greedy selection rule with acceleration and stochastic optimization to efficiently solve l1-regularized problems.

paragraphs: Private learning usually starts with a privacy requirement and seeks the most accurate result that satisfies it. This paper reverses that priority: an analyst specifies an accuracy requirement, and the method searches for the strongest privacy level that can meet it. The setting is empirical risk minimization, which fits a model by minimizing an objective evaluated on the data.

The authors propose a general noise-reduction framework that works with a variety of private learning algorithms. It searches across privacy levels to find the empirically strongest one satisfying the accuracy constraint, with overhead that grows only logarithmically in the number of levels searched. This makes the search itself part of the privacy analysis.

That analysis introduces ex-post privacy, in which privacy parameters depend on the data, and connects it to privacy odometers. The authors also adapt and analyze the AboveThreshold tool for database-dependent queries. Applications to regularized linear and logistic regression compare the framework empirically with methods based on theoretical accuracy guarantees and with a binary-search baseline.
neurips-2017-accuracy-first-selecting-a-.tldr: A noise-reduction framework searches for the empirically strongest privacy level that meets a specified learning accuracy requirement.

paragraphs: Dropout can help large neural networks estimate uncertainty, but the probability of dropping units affects how well those estimates are calibrated. The paper identifies manual grid search over these probabilities as a major obstacle: it is prohibitively expensive for large models and described as infeasible for reinforcement learning.

Concrete Dropout makes the dropout probability tunable during optimization. Its central mechanism replaces discrete dropout masks with a continuous relaxation. Combined with an optimization objective grounded in Bayesian deep learning, this allows the model to adjust dropout probabilities automatically. The practical benefit is a shorter experimentation cycle because those probabilities no longer require the same external search.

The authors report improved performance and better-calibrated uncertainty across a range of tasks. In reinforcement learning, automatic adjustment also lets an agent change its uncertainty as it observes more data. Their analysis examines the common practice of assigning larger dropout probabilities to deeper layers, providing insight into a design choice that is otherwise often set manually.
neurips-2017-concrete-dropout-a35449fe98.tldr: Concrete Dropout learns dropout probabilities through a continuous relaxation, improving reported performance and uncertainty calibration.

paragraphs: Topological data analysis summarizes aspects of the shape and structure of data. Methods such as persistent homology produce signatures that can complement other information used in machine learning. However, these summaries may take unusual forms, including collections of intervals, that ordinary learning methods cannot readily accept as inputs.

Existing conversion strategies make these signatures easier to use but typically do not adapt the representation to the prediction task. The paper introduces a neural-network input layer that accepts topological signatures and learns their representation during training. This lets the task influence which aspects of the signature become useful features, rather than fixing that conversion independently of learning.

The authors establish favorable theoretical properties for the layer and evaluate it on classification of two-dimensional object shapes and social network graphs. These experiments demonstrate use across different kinds of structured data. For the social network graph task, they report a large improvement over the state of the art. The main contribution is a trainable connection between topological summaries and deep learning.
neurips-2017-deep-learning-with-topologi.tldr: A trainable input layer lets deep networks adapt topological signatures to their task, with strong reported graph-classification results.

paragraphs: Patients with multiple conditions may face several competing adverse outcomes, making cause-specific prognosis important for treatment planning. This paper develops a Bayesian survival model that jointly assesses these risks. It uses patient characteristics as inputs and represents survival times for the competing outcomes through a deep multi-task Gaussian process.

The approach is designed to capture complex nonlinear relationships between patient characteristics and cause-specific survival times. It learns survival curves that vary both by patient and by outcome, without imposing explicit parametric forms on hazard rates. This flexibility is the main distinction drawn from the Cox- and Weibull-based parametric approaches discussed in the abstract.

The authors introduce a variational inference algorithm for learning from time-to-event records while accounting for right censoring, where observation ends before the event occurs. Experiments on synthetic and real data show better performance than the state-of-the-art survival models considered. The findings support flexible joint prognosis for competing risks; the reported evaluation concerns prediction rather than demonstrated improvements in treatment outcomes.
neurips-2017-deep-multi-task-gaussian-pr.tldr: A deep multi-task Gaussian process learns flexible patient-specific survival curves for competing risks while handling censored observations.

paragraphs: GAN training involves a generator and a discriminator learning together, which makes convergence a central concern. This paper proposes a two time-scale update rule, TTUR, that gives the two components separate learning rates. The rule is formulated for stochastic gradient training with arbitrary GAN loss functions.

Using stochastic approximation theory, the authors prove convergence to a stationary local Nash equilibrium under mild assumptions. The guarantee concerns a local equilibrium and remains conditional on those assumptions. They extend the convergence result to Adam and analyze that optimizer through the dynamics of a heavy ball with friction, arguing that these dynamics favor flat minima.

The paper also introduces Fréchet Inception Distance, or FID, to evaluate generated images, reporting that it captures similarity to real images better than Inception Score. Experiments show improved learning for DCGAN and WGAN-GP compared with conventional training across several image datasets and the One Billion Word Benchmark. The work therefore contributes both a training rule with conditional theoretical support and an evaluation measure for generated images.
neurips-2017-gans-trained-by-a-two-time-.tldr: TTUR uses separate GAN learning rates, proves conditional convergence to a local Nash equilibrium, and introduces FID for image evaluation.

paragraphs: Wasserstein GANs aim to improve the stability of adversarial training, yet they can still produce poor samples or fail to converge. This paper identifies weight clipping as a frequent source of those problems. Clipping is used to enforce a Lipschitz constraint on the critic, but the authors find that it can induce undesirable behavior.

Their alternative penalizes the norm of the critic's gradient with respect to its input. This changes how the critic is constrained: the training objective directly penalizes its input-gradient behavior instead of relying on clipped weights. The proposal targets a particular mechanism behind WGAN instability rather than changing the overall generator-and-critic setup.

The authors report better performance than standard WGAN and stable training across a broad range of architectures with almost no hyperparameter tuning. Demonstrations include 101-layer residual networks and language models with continuous generators, alongside high-quality image generation on CIFAR-10 and LSUN bedrooms. These results provide empirical support for the gradient penalty as a broadly useful training modification.
neurips-2017-improved-training-of-wasser.tldr: Replacing WGAN weight clipping with an input-gradient penalty improves reported training stability and generation quality across diverse architectures.

paragraphs: Compressive image recovery seeks to reconstruct images from compressed measurements. Neural networks offer fast reconstruction, but the paper identifies difficulties with training, interpretability, and dependence on a single measurement matrix. The authors build a network around an existing iterative recovery algorithm to give the learned system a more explicit structure.

Learned D-AMP, or LDAMP, mimics denoising-based approximate message passing. Inspired by turning iterative algorithms into network layers, this architecture connects learned reconstruction to an established computational procedure. The authors describe it as easy to train and applicable to different measurement matrices. They also provide a state-evolution heuristic that accurately predicts performance; this predictive tool is presented as a heuristic.

LDAMP outperforms BM3D-AMP and NLR-CS in both reconstruction accuracy and runtime in the reported comparisons. At high image resolutions, when the sensing matrices have fast implementations, it runs more than 50 times faster than BM3D-AMP and hundreds of times faster than NLR-CS. Those conditions are part of the large speedup claim.
neurips-2017-learned-d-amp-principled-ne.tldr: LDAMP turns a denoising-based recovery algorithm into a trainable network with improved reported reconstruction accuracy and runtime.

paragraphs: This paper considers convex optimization over a trace-norm ball, a matrix constraint, and modifies the classical Frank-Wolfe algorithm for that setting. Its central idea is to use information from the top k singular vectors at each update, replacing the single leading singular-vector computation used by standard Frank-Wolfe.

The larger singular-vector computation can be carried out by repeating the single-vector procedure k times. The authors also give another interpretation of the method: it is projected gradient descent restricted to rank k. These two views connect the proposed algorithm to familiar optimization approaches while making the role of the rank parameter explicit.

The convergence guarantee depends on concrete conditions. The objective must be smooth and strongly convex, and the optimal solution must have rank no greater than k. Under those conditions, the method converges linearly, improving both the convergence rate and total time complexity over Frank-Wolfe and its variants. The result shows how matching the update rank to the solution's rank can support faster optimization.
neurips-2017-linear-convergence-of-a-fra.tldr: A rank-k Frank-Wolfe variant converges linearly for smooth, strongly convex objectives when the optimum has rank at most k.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization when evaluating both the objective and the constraints is expensive. A useful solution must improve the objective while also satisfying inequality constraints. Bayesian optimization addresses costly evaluations, but the authors identify a limitation in existing constrained approaches: they choose evaluations according to immediate reward.

The proposed method looks further ahead. It chooses the next evaluation to maximize the long-term reduction of the objective that remains feasible under the constraints. This changes the decision being optimized from immediate progress to progress over a longer horizon. Because constraint evaluations are also costly, deciding where to evaluate involves more than simply seeking a favorable objective value.

Numerical experiments compare the lookahead approach with several greedy Bayesian optimization algorithms, including constrained expected improvement and predictive entropy search with constraints. The authors report performance improvements in those experiments. The findings support considering longer-term feasible gains when choosing expensive evaluations, while the abstract presents this advantage as an experimental result rather than a universal dominance guarantee.
neurips-2017-lookahead-bayesian-optimiza.tldr: A lookahead Bayesian optimizer targets long-term feasible improvement and outperforms several greedy constrained methods in numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Brain activity unfolds over many timescales, so understanding connections between regions requires attention to both timing and spatial organization. This paper examines whether instantaneous and lag-based Granger-Geweke measures can identify distinct functional interactions in fMRI data. It challenges the view that fMRI's slow sampling necessarily makes these measures unreliable.

The authors first use simulated fMRI data to examine what the two types of measure capture. Their results show distinct timescales and complementary connectivity patterns. They then analyze scans from 500 subjects and train linear classifiers to distinguish task-related brain states from rest using either instantaneous or lag-based connectivity.

Both types of connectivity support approximately 80–85% cross-validation accuracy. However, the classifiers draw on markedly different spatial and temporal patterns. This distinction matters because similar classification performance can reflect different information about brain networks. Together, the simulations and classification results support using the measures to identify functional networks operating at different timescales; the reported connections concern functional dependence in the analyzed data.
neurips-2017-mapping-distinct-timescales.tldr: Instantaneous and lag-based fMRI connectivity measures capture complementary patterns and distinguish task from rest with about 80–85% cross-validation accuracy.

paragraphs: A matrix's singular values reveal information about its structure and effective dimensionality. In applications where only some entries are observed, recovering that information can be difficult. This paper asks whether useful spectral summaries can be estimated directly from partial observations without first reconstructing the entire matrix.

The proposed framework estimates Schatten k-norms for several choices of k. These norms summarize singular-value information and serve as substitutes for estimating properties such as rank or the spectrum. The technical contribution is an unbiased estimator built by counting small structures in a graph. The authors provide theoretical guarantees that align with its observed empirical behavior.

The analysis shows that accurate Schatten-norm estimation can require strictly fewer sampled entries than recovery of the underlying low-rank matrix. This separates the information needed for a structural summary from the information needed for full reconstruction. Numerical experiments also suggest substantial improvement over an approach based on matrix completion, supporting the value of estimating the desired summaries directly.
neurips-2017-matrix-norm-estimation-from.tldr: Graph-based unbiased estimators recover matrix norm summaries from fewer observations than are needed to reconstruct the underlying low-rank matrix.

paragraphs: Gaussian process regression becomes difficult to scale beyond a few thousand observations without approximating its kernel matrix. The paper identifies a weakness in common approximations: they concentrate on the part of the matrix spectrum associated with large eigenvalues. According to the abstract, this focus produces poor performance when the kernel length scale is small.

The authors introduce Multiresolution Kernel Approximation, or MKA, as a broad-bandwidth alternative. The motivation is to address a wider range of the kernel spectrum instead of concentrating approximation effort on its largest eigenvalues. This targets the particular spectral imbalance that the paper associates with difficulties at small length scales.

MKA is described as memory efficient and as a direct method. Its direct form also makes it easy to approximate the inverse and determinant of the kernel matrix. These capabilities broaden what the approximation provides beyond an approximate matrix alone. The contribution is therefore a kernel approximation designed around spectral coverage, storage efficiency, and access to additional matrix quantities useful in Gaussian process regression.
neurips-2017-multiresolution-kernel-appr.tldr: MKA offers a memory-efficient, broad-bandwidth kernel approximation that also facilitates approximate matrix inverses and determinants.

paragraphs: The paper studies online prediction with expert advice as a game between a learner and an adversary. Its focus is minimax behavior: strategies that characterize the best achievable performance against a worst-case opponent. A simple adversary called COMB had been conjectured to be nearly optimal for any number of experts.

The authors establish progress on that conjecture for exactly three experts over a finite number of rounds. They show that COMB is minimax optimal up to a small additive term and construct a corresponding learner that is also nearly minimax optimal. The result addresses both sides of the game within this specific setting.

For T rounds, the game's regret is characterized by sqrt(8T/(9π)), with an additive discrepancy bounded by log(T)^2. This identifies the optimal coefficient of the leading square-root term. Previously, learners achieving the optimal leading coefficient were known only for two experts or in the limit of infinitely many experts. The contribution resolves that coefficient for the finite three-expert case.
neurips-2017-near-minimax-optimal-player.tldr: For three experts, the paper gives nearly minimax-optimal adversary and learner strategies and determines the optimal leading regret constant.

paragraphs: The paper studies influence spreading through a network under the independent cascade model. The quantity of interest is the expected number of nodes reached from an initial seed set. Instead of providing only a single estimate, the authors develop both upper and lower bounds on that expected reach.

Their bounds combine nonbacktracking walks with Fortuin-Kasteleyn-Ginibre-type inequalities and are computed through message passing. A nonbacktracking walk avoids immediately reversing the edge just traversed. The paper brings this way of tracking network paths, already useful in community detection, into the computation of influence. The inequalities and path structure together support the bounding approach.

The authors also introduce parameterized versions that let the computation trade efficiency against accuracy. This gives a way to adjust how much computational effort is spent tightening the bounds. Simulations on several network models illustrate their tightness. The contribution is thus a family of computable bounds, with adjustable computational cost and empirical demonstrations of how closely they constrain expected influence.
neurips-2017-nonbacktracking-bounds-on-t.tldr: Message-passing algorithms use nonbacktracking walks to bound expected network influence, with an adjustable efficiency–accuracy trade-off.

paragraphs: This paper examines how truncated singular value decomposition can help estimate matrices that are not exactly low rank. Its starting point is a high-rank positive semidefinite matrix and an initial estimate that is close in spectral norm. The authors show that truncating the estimate's singular value decomposition yields a multiplicative approximation in Frobenius norm.

The distinction between these error measures drives the applications: a spectral-norm guarantee on an initial estimate can be turned into a relative Frobenius-norm approximation. For high-rank matrix completion, the authors obtain a 1+epsilon relative-error result from partial observations with sample complexity independent of the spectral gap. They also develop denoising algorithms without requiring an exactly low-rank target.

A further application concerns covariance estimation from independent, identically distributed zero-mean Gaussian samples in n dimensions. The authors show that relative Frobenius error can be achieved with approximately n samples, compared with the approximately n-squared requirement of the classical results they discuss. The Gaussian sampling setting is part of this covariance claim.
neurips-2017-on-the-power-of-truncated-s.tldr: Truncated SVD converts spectral-norm accuracy into relative Frobenius-norm guarantees, enabling results for high-rank completion, denoising, and covariance estimation.

paragraphs: Online learning evaluates decisions as information arrives over time. This paper broadens the notion of regret by allowing comparison rules to modify sequences of expert choices rather than only individual experts. The resulting measure, transductive regret, considers modifications that can be represented by weighted finite-state transducers.

This sequence-based formulation includes external, internal, swap, and conditional swap regret within one framework. Its value is that several established comparison criteria become instances of a more general problem. The authors give an efficient online learning algorithm for minimizing this broader regret, so the unification comes with an algorithmic method as well as a definition.

They extend the approach to time-selection and sleeping-expert settings, addressing additional structure in when comparisons or experts are relevant. The framework also produces a swap-regret algorithm that is more efficient than existing alternatives under mild assumptions, plus a substantially more efficient algorithm for time-selection swap regret. These results show how the general formulation can improve algorithms for familiar special cases.
neurips-2017-online-learning-with-transd.tldr: Transductive regret unifies several online-learning regret notions through sequence transformations and yields efficient algorithms for general and specialized settings.

paragraphs: An image contains both individual objects and relationships between them. A graph can represent these two kinds of information together, making it a useful description of a scene. This paper develops a convolutional neural network that takes an image as input and outputs a complete graph definition.

The method uses associative embeddings to identify the graph's constituent elements and connect them. Both jobs are learned together in a single stage, with training carried out end to end. This joint formulation makes assembling the graph part of the network's learned task, alongside recognizing the elements that need to appear in it.

The authors evaluate the system on Visual Genome and report state-of-the-art performance for scene graph generation. The result supports the use of associative embeddings for producing structured descriptions directly from images. More broadly, the paper demonstrates a concrete way for an image-processing network to output interconnected scene information, extending its output beyond a collection of separately identified objects.
neurips-2017-pixels-to-graphs-by-associa.tldr: A single-stage convolutional network uses associative embeddings to jointly identify and connect scene-graph elements from an image.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning when the true environment is unavailable and learning relies on a reasonably close approximation. This mismatch matters because decisions are learned from an environment that does not exactly match the target. The authors extend robust Markov decision processes to a model-free setting where sampling is possible but model parameters are inaccessible.

They define robust versions of Q-learning, Sarsa, and temporal-difference learning. Their convergence results establish an approximately optimal robust policy and an approximate value function, respectively. The approximation qualifications are part of the results: the aim is reliable learning under model mismatch rather than exact recovery of behavior in the true environment.

For larger problems, the authors use function approximation and prove convergence in two settings. One covers robust approximate policy and value iteration with linear architectures under mild assumptions. The other introduces a mean squared robust projected Bellman error and stochastic gradient algorithms guaranteed to reach a local minimum. These provide distinct routes for extending robust learning beyond small state spaces.
neurips-2017-reinforcement-learning-unde.tldr: Robust model-free learning algorithms provide qualified convergence guarantees when training uses an approximate environment.

paragraphs: Choosing reserve prices in advertising auctions is difficult because advertising opportunities differ and the revenue objective is nonconvex. This paper connects that difficult optimization task to a more familiar learning problem: predicting bids under squared loss. The connection provides a way to approach reserve-price selection through a standard prediction objective.

The main methodological result is a reduction from reserve-price optimization to squared-loss prediction. This matters because it relates the auction decision to a well-understood form of machine learning. The contribution is not merely to suggest that accurate predictions might help; it establishes a formal relationship between predictive quality and revenue.

Specifically, the authors bound the difference between the expected bid and revenue using the predictor's average loss. That bound explains how prediction error enters a revenue guarantee. It connects a quantity used to assess a learned predictor with a quantity relevant to auction performance. The abstract presents this as the first formal link between revenue gained and the quality of a standard machine-learned model.
neurips-2017-revenue-optimization-with-a.tldr: The paper reduces auction reserve-price optimization to squared-loss prediction and bounds the expected-bid–revenue gap using prediction error.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to learn representations that are suitable for compression within deep architectures. The goal is to make compressibility part of end-to-end training. The method centers on quantization and entropy, using continuous versions of these quantities during the learning process.

The approach begins with soft relaxations and gradually anneals them toward their discrete counterparts. This creates a progression from a continuous training formulation to the discrete representations required by the compression approach. The same progression applies to both quantization and entropy, bringing the representation and its compression-related objective into a shared training strategy.

The authors demonstrate the method on image compression and neural-network compression, two applications usually handled by different techniques. They report results competitive with the state of the art in both. The significance is the reach of a common learning approach across these distinct compression targets. The stated findings support competitiveness and a unified training strategy, without claiming that the method surpasses every specialized alternative.
neurips-2017-soft-to-hard-vector-quantiz.tldr: Gradually converting soft quantization and entropy into discrete forms enables competitive end-to-end image and neural-network compression.

paragraphs: Distributed neural-network training can spend substantial time communicating gradients and parameters between workers. TernGrad targets this bottleneck in data-parallel training by representing gradients with three numerical levels: minus one, zero, and one. This compact representation can greatly reduce the time needed to communicate training updates.

The authors prove convergence under an assumption that gradients satisfy a bound. Guided by that condition, they introduce layer-wise ternarization and gradient clipping to improve convergence. The theoretical guarantee therefore depends on a stated gradient assumption, while the implementation choices are motivated by the same analysis.

Experiments show no accuracy loss for AlexNet and, in some cases, improved accuracy. For GoogLeNet, the reported average accuracy loss is below 2%. The authors also propose a performance model to study scalability and report significant speed gains across several deep networks. These findings show that reduced communication can translate into faster training, with the observed effect on accuracy varying between the tested architectures.
neurips-2017-terngrad-ternary-gradients-.tldr: TernGrad compresses communicated gradients to three levels, yielding reported training speedups with architecture-dependent accuracy effects.

paragraphs: The paper identifies a conflict in GANs used for semi-supervised learning: a single discriminator may be asked both to detect generated examples and to predict class labels. These roles can be incompatible, and a generator that does not model labels cannot directly control the classes of its outputs.

Triple-GAN separates the system into three players: a generator, a classifier, and a discriminator. The generator and classifier model conditional relationships between images and labels, while the discriminator judges image-label pairs. The authors design compatible objectives to ensure that the distributions represented by the generator and classifier both converge to the data distribution.

Experiments across several datasets report state-of-the-art classification performance among deep generative models. The same model also separates class information from style and supports smooth changes through latent-space interpolation while conditioning on a class. The contribution is a unified formulation that supports both classification and controllable generation by giving these functions distinct roles within the adversarial system.
neurips-2017-triple-generative-adversari.tldr: Triple-GAN separates generation, classification, and discrimination to jointly support semi-supervised classification and class-controlled image generation.

paragraphs: This paper seeks to learn meaningful image transformations without supervision. Examples include changing the thickness of handwriting strokes or altering lighting in a portrait. The objective is to extract transformations from raw images so that learned changes correspond to recognizable visual variation.

The method attempts to reconstruct an image as a linear combination of transformed versions of its nearest neighbors. Learning transformations is therefore tied to explaining how nearby examples can combine to reproduce an observed image. The authors demonstrate that even linear transformations can produce visually high-quality image modifications on handwritten digits and celebrity portraits.

The approach is semiparametric and does not model the overall data distribution. The authors connect this design to the ability of learned transformations to extrapolate beyond the training data and operate on new types of images. This extends their usefulness beyond modifying examples similar to those used in training. The stated findings concern visually meaningful modifications and transferable transformations, rather than a claim that every learned change generalizes to every image.
neurips-2017-unsupervised-transformation.tldr: An unsupervised reconstruction approach learns meaningful image transformations that produce high-quality modifications and can transfer to new image types.
